First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨{e}^{t}-4,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t}-4,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int ({e}^{t}-4)\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}-4t+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}-4t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}-4t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

questions.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩\text{d}t=⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)={e}^{t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\text{d}t={e}^{t}+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =2(-\operatorname{cos}⁡u)+{c}_{2} \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{e}^{t}+{c}_{1},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the following integral of a vector-valued function. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{1}^{8}⟨5t-2,\,\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{t}^{2}}}⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨$
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $⟩$
questions.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{8}⟨5t-2,\,\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{t}^{2}}}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{1}^{8}(5t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,{\int }_{1}^{8}\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{t}^{2}}}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

For the first component, we integrate directly:

$$
\int (5t-2)\,\text{d}t=\frac{5}{2}{t}^{2}-2t.
$$

For the second component, we write 

$$
\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{t}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{3}{t}^{-2/3}
$$

and integrate:

$$
\int \frac{1}{3}{t}^{-2/3}\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{{t}^{1/3}}{1/3}={t}^{1/3}.
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{8}⟨5t-2,\,\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{t}^{2}}}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨(\frac{5}{2}{t}^{2}-2t){|}_{1}^{8},\,({t}^{1/3}){|}_{1}^{8}⟩ \\  & =⟨(\frac{5}{2}\cdot 64-16)-(\frac{5}{2}\cdot 1-2),\,2-1⟩ \\  & =⟨144-\frac{1}{2},\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{287}{2},\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{287}{2},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨3(t-1)^{2},\,4{t}^{3}-1⟩\text{d}t
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨3(t-1)^{2},\,4{t}^{3}-1⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 3(t-1)^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (4{t}^{3}-1)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{(t-1)}^{3}+{c}_{1},\,{t}^{4}-t+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨1,\,1⟩$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨{((1)-1)}^{3}+{c}_{1},\,(1)^{4}-(1)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=1.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨{(t-1)}^{3}+1,\,{t}^{4}-t+1⟩.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\sqrt{t}+t,\,{2}^{t}⟩\text{d}t
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\sqrt{t}+t,\,{2}^{t}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (\sqrt{t}+t)\,\text{d}t,\int {2}^{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{{2}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

   

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨2,\,0⟩$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨\frac{2(1)^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{{2}^{1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{7}{6}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=\frac{5}{6}$ and ${c}_{2}=-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$ Consequently

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =⟨\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{5}{6},\,\frac{{2}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{4{t}^{3/2}+3{t}^{2}+5}{6},\,\frac{{2}^{t}-2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find $\mathbf F(t)$ given that $\mathbf F'(t)= \langle 6t^5+2t, \sec^2 t\rangle.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle 6t^5+2t,\, \sec^2 t\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨6{t}^{5}+2t,\,{sec}^{2}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int (6{t}^{5}+2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int {sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2}+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbf C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t) =\cos(2t+1),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u= 2t +1.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d t} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d t = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t) =4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t=\int 4\text{d}t=4t+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1},\,4t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Definite Integral of a Vector-Valued Function
Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\mathbf F(t)$ given that $\mathbf F'(t)= \left\langle \sec t \tan t, \,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf F(0)=\langle 0,\, 0\rangle.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle \sec t \tan t,\,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $\mathbf F(0)=\left\langle 0,\, 0 \right\rangle$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0)=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡0+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨1+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $c_1=-1$ and $c_2=\dfrac 12.$ Consequently, 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\left\langle  \sec t - 1  , \,  -\dfrac 1 2\cos(2t)+ \dfrac12\right\rangle.
$$
